I think we should redefine docs#eLpNorm to be ∞ when the function is not docs#MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable.
Currently the value for non-measurable f is "the supremum of ‖g‖_{L^p} for measurable g that a.e. satisfy ‖g‖ ≤ ‖f‖".

The reason for this is twofold:

  • I think it's a slightly better junk value. It means that some results can be stated without measurability assumption, e.g. docs#MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_add_le will be true unconditionally. Of course, there will be other results that need an additional assumption, e.g. docs#MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_mono_ae.
  • I think it plays a lot better with docs#MeasureTheory.MemLp, which could be redefined as eLpNorm f p μ < ∞ in the new situation. I think it's much nicer if all non-L^p functions have infinite L^p norm.

One thing I'm not sure about is whether the L^0 norm should be constantly 0 or also ∞ for non-measurable functions.

Thoughts? (cc @Yury G. Kudryashov, @Sébastien Gouëzel, @Rémy Degenne)
Very good idea

To elaborate on the second point: this ensures that all the information is captured by the norm. I think this will be very useful if we want to consider operations on seminorms/quasinorms, such as abstract interpolation theory (a very preliminary experiment is here)
I agree it's probably a good idea.

Floris van Doorn said:

One thing I'm not sure about is whether the L^0 norm should be constantly 0 or also ∞ for non-measurable functions.

Is the fact that the L^0 norm is 0 actually used anywhere?
Not intentionally, but we should probably make a choice that results in the fewest p \ne 0 hypotheses.
This isn't specifically about non-measurable functions, but would it make sense to actually define it in terms of the limiting behavior of L^p seminorms as p goes to 0?

Some time ago, I wanted to redefine the norm so that

  • we drop the outer (_)^(1/p) for 0 < p < 1
  • we use the measure of support f for p = 0
    but I failed to finish the refactor before it rot.
This :up: would allow us to drop Fact (1 ≤ p) here and there.
E.g., we get a SeminormedGroup for any p, but it's a p-norm.
That would have the benefit of generalizing of the existing meanings of the 'L^0 norm' in the literature (i.e., the L^0 norm of of a vector in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn being the number of non-zero entries).

James E Hanson said:

That would have the benefit of generalizing of the existing meanings of the 'L^0 norm' in the literature (i.e., the L^0 norm of of a vector in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn being the number of non-zero entries).

This formula depends on the specific choice of coordinates you are using, while the other L^p norms are invariant under linear maps preserving the volume (and are in particular coordinate independent), so I don't see how they could play well together.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

James E Hanson said:

That would have the benefit of generalizing of the existing meanings of the 'L^0 norm' in the literature (i.e., the L^0 norm of of a vector in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn being the number of non-zero entries).

This formula depends on the specific choice of coordinates you are using, while the other L^p norms are invariant under linear maps preserving the volume (and are in particular coordinate independent), so I don't see how they could play well together.

When I say the seminorm is 'on' Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, I mean that Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn is the corresponding vector space, not the corresponding measure space. In that example, the measure space in question is the measure space with nnn elements and the counting measure.
Ah, thanks for clarifying!
Although now I just realized that in Mathlib 0 ^ 0 = 1 in ℝ, so it wouldn't immediately match the definition I mentioned.
Ah, but this is already covered by Yury's proposal.
(I am now working on this, first PR should come soon)
#39311 now implements the change for p=0 (rather big refactor).

Yury G. Kudryashov said:

  • we drop the outer (_)^(1/p) for 0 < p < 1

For posterity: Terence Tao mentioned that we shouldn't use a mixed convention where this choice is different for p<1p<1p<1 and p>1p>1p>1, since then Holder's inequality will fail when mixing these two cases.
Instead, we should have both norms in the library.

To have both, I'm wondering if we should parametrize the norm by two numbers, the inner exponent ppp and the outer exponent p′p'p′, and then the two choices are (p,p′):=(p,1/p)(p,p'):=(p,1/p)(p,p′):=(p,1/p) and (p,p′):=(p,1)(p,p'):=(p, 1)(p,p′):=(p,1).
Are there other interesting cases considered in the literature? I am just wondering, it's a good idea anyway.

I just want to mention that one reason for Yury's proposal is that, if we drop the power 1/p when p < 1, then Lp becomes a NormedAddCommGroup in all cases. Given how Mathlib typeclasses in analysis are designed, this definitely looks like the right move (if we keep the 1/p, then we don't have a NormedAddCommGroup, and then we can't have a NormedSpace either as it depends on the former one). However, having two bare functions -- the current eLpNorm' that keeps the 1/p, and another one that drops it when p < 1, is definitely a good idea.
Note that Hölder inequality is typically stated and used at the level of functions, not ae classes of functions, so the norm we choose for the typeclasses is not really relevant here.

(passing comment that these spaces showed up in the liquid tensor experiment together with what seemed to be the correct version of "normed space" in that situation:


)
CC: @Terence Tao
I don't understand why we don't simply add QuasiNormedAddCommGroup. Spaces with such norm arise in other contexts besides simply Lp spaces.

One may end up having three bundled versions of L^p in addition to the unbundled versions:

  1. MetricLp types that come with a NormedAddCommGroup type structure, splitting into p<1 and p≥1 as needed.
  2. Lp that comes with Jireh's proposed QuasiNormedAddCommGroup structure (EDIT: which should be inherited from Kevin/Peter's pBanachSpace structure) in which one treats all p uniformly. This is the setting where Holder's inequality naturally lives.
  3. BanachLp that also comes with a bundled hypothesis p≥1 and has a BanachSpace structure.

With enough coercion API between the three types I think things are workable. Most statements about LpL^pLp spaces should naturally fit live in the above three bundled types.

@Floris van Doorn, there is a (minor?) issue with the double index approach. Note that if you have p and p' that are equal, but not definitionally, you'll need an equiv to go between the bundled versions of docs#MeasureTheory.Lp. If you add a second argument, you will need to do this transition more frequently, especially because there are more ways to write 1/p.

Here's a thing we could do: define an inductive type that has two constructors, and make this another argument to WithLp, but also provide a default argument. Then nothing needs to change in Mathlib right now at all (except the definition of WithLp), but we can also have the quasinormed variant. This is akin to what we did for HasSum.

Terence Tao said:

One may end up having three bundled versions of L^p in addition to the unbundled versions:

  1. MetricLp types that come with a NormedAddCommGroup type structure, splitting into p<1 and p≥1 as needed.
  2. Lp that comes with Jireh's proposed QuasiNormedAddCommGroup structure (EDIT: which should be inherited from Kevin/Peter's pBanachSpace structure) in which one treats all p uniformly. This is the setting where Holder's inequality naturally lives.
  3. BanachLp that also comes with a bundled hypothesis p≥1 and has a BanachSpace structure.

Why do we need 3? Isn't it covered by either/both 1 and 2?

The classes 1. and 2. don't automatically come with a BanachSpace structure. Also one has to decide whether BanachLp extends Lp or MetricLp; one cannot do both as this would create an instance diamond (e.g., with Norm or dist). If we didn't have a canonical such space, and allowed different Mathlib contributors to build BanachSpace structure from either 1. or 2. as they chose, then at some point there is going to be a defeq or instance diamond issue when trying to use two different results about Lp spaces in the Banach space setting (which is the majority, though not the overwhelming majority, of Lp applications).
Terry, that's not really problem. Completeness isn't data, so there's no need to worry about diamonds / distinct instances. And we handle the instancification with Fact (1 /le p)
Completeness might be fine, but Norm carries data and so still might cause an issue if we truly want to support both types of norm like structures on Lp.

The reason for this is twofold:

  • I think it's a slightly better junk value. It means that some results can be stated without measurability assumption, e.g. docs#MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_add_le will be true unconditionally. Of course, there will be other results that need an additional assumption, e.g. docs#MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_mono_ae.

Thoughts? (cc Yury G. Kudryashov, Sébastien Gouëzel, Rémy Degenne)

Does this mean that we no longer need any APIs related to MeasureTheory.Integrable? As if we set eLpNorm f p μ = ∞ for any nonaestronglymeasurable functions then Integrable is the same as HasFiniteIntegral.

I am not against this, I just want to point out that this sounds like a huge change.

HasFiniteIntegral is about the requirement that ∫⁻ a, ‖f a‖ₑ ∂μ < ∞, it is not about the eLpNorm 1. Even if we change the meaning of eLpNorm (and I think that's a good idea), we wouldn't touch the definition of HasFiniteIntegral.
But doesn't MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_one_eq_lintegral_enorm say that eLpNorm 1 is exactly ∫⁻ a, ‖f a‖ₑ ∂μ?
I believe Aaron is correct here (i.e., that HasFiniteIntegral \iff Integrable) after the proposed change.

For me, the proposed change would be that the new definition of eLpNorm would give eLpNorm f 1 mu = if AEStronglyMeasurable f mu then ∫⁻ a, ‖f a‖ₑ ∂μ else ∞. But we would not change the definition of ∫⁻ a, ‖f a‖ₑ ∂μ. So having finite integral would not change, and would not imply ae strong measurability.

Yongxi Lin (Aaron) said:

But doesn't MeasureTheory.eLpNorm_one_eq_lintegral_enorm say that eLpNorm 1 is exactly ∫⁻ a, ‖f a‖ₑ ∂μ?

Aha, the point is that with the new definition of eLpNorm this theorem would need a measurability hypothesis.

I wonder if @Floris van Doorn can confirm whether Sébastien Gouëzel's interpretation matches Floris' intended change. It seems so to me now, but it would be good to make sure we're all on the same page.

Jireh Loreaux said:

I wonder if Floris van Doorn can confirm whether Sébastien Gouëzel's interpretation matches Floris' intended change. It seems so to me now, but it would be good to make sure we're all on the same page.

Yes, this was the change I also intended with my message.

There is a very nice PR by @Felix Pernegger at #39311 starting on this, by redefining the eLpNorm at p=0. Before rushing to merge it, I think it's worth anticipating a little bit on what we would like to have as a final stage, to make sure that the PR fits in this plan.

One possibility is the following: to have two functions, say eLpNormHomogeneous f p μ (with a better name) and eLpNorm f p μ, defined as follows:

  • eLpNormHomogeneous f p μ is the current eLpNorm, i.e., 0 at p = 0, and (∫⁻ x, ‖f x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ)^(1/p) at finite nonzero p, and the esssup of f at infinity
  • eLpNorm f p μ is infinity for non-AEStronglyMeasurable functions. For AEStronglyMeasurable functions, it is the measure of the support for p = 0, it is ∫⁻ x, ‖f x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ for 0 < p < 1, it is (∫⁻ x, ‖f x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ)^(1/p) for 1 \le p < top, and it is the esssup at infinity.

In this way,

  • eLpNormHomogeneous f p μ is homogeneous (i.e., the norm of c f is |c| times the norm of f), and can be used to write Hölder-like inequalities in the greatest generality
  • eLpNorm is always an additive norm (i.e., the norm of f + g is bounded by the sum of the norms of f and g), and L^p is exactly the space of (equivalence classes of) functions for which eLpNorm is finite. It can be used to endow L^p with a normed add comm group structure for all p, which improves to a normed space structure for 1 \le p.

Thoughts? Weaknesses? Better ideas?
I really don't think we should be doing a case split to define the norm. I think what we want there is a definition of quasinormed space.
For p = 0 you don't even have a quasinormed space, but you still have a normed add comm group.

It's not clear to me what the best endpoint should be. It's annoying to have two conventions of LpL^pLp-norms around, but maybe/probably we'll have to resort to that.

@Sébastien Gouëzel: in your proposal, is there a reason that eLpNormHomogeneous should be 0 for p = 0 and finite for (some) non-measurable functions? I hoped that these two conventions wouldn't be problematic for either choice of LpL^pLp-norm.

We could definitely make eLpNormHomogeneous infinite for non-aestronglyMeasurableFunctions, for coherence with the other version. In this way, for p different from 0 then L^p would also exactly be the functions with finite eLpNormHomogeneous.

I'm happy with Sebastien's proposal to have the normed structure be the default recommended structure and the homogeneous quasi-normed structure be the alternate structure in situations where homogeneity is more important than the metric structure (Holder's inequality with exponents below 1 being the primary case in which this occurs, but there may be others). Analysis textbooks tend to emphasize the homogeneous norm, but perhaps part of the value of formalization is revealing subtle optimizations to the textbook definitions.

Unfortunately (per review by @Sébastien Gouëzel ), my PR #39311 which ought to be the first refactor, is not optimal towards the eventual plan (i.e. having two eLpNorms) and probably cannot be merged due to that.

However I want to continue with refactoring eLpNorm; so I am wondering (to prevent the same thing from happening again) whether the original suggestion, changing the junk value to infinity if the function is not `AEStronglyMeasurable, is uncontroversial and can be done now in any case?

Note that this will require eLpNorm to also take the argument TopologicalSpace ε.

Yes, sorry about that. Let me copy the message I've written on your PR, as others may have thoughts on the refactoring process:

the endgoal of the refactor could be the following:

  • one function eLpHmgNorm, the homogeneous L^p norm, which correspond to the current eLpNorm (except that it would be infinite for non aestronglyMeasurable functions) and satisfies eLpHmgNorm (c • f) p μ = ‖c‖₊ • eLpHmgNorm f p μ.
  • another function eLpNorm which would be homogeneous only for p ≥ 1, but would be a seminorm for all p. This is the one that would be used to put the normed structure on L^p, to make sure we have a distance, a topology and everything.

What your refactor is doing is changing some part of the current eLpNorm, to replace its behavior at p = 0 by the new one. However, I am afraid it will make part of the refactor harder, because some theorems will hold for all values of p for eLpHmgNorm, and to get these we will need to undo what you're doing in the PR.

A tentative plan to get the refactor done while not doing everything at once could be:
(1) modify the current definition of eLpNorm to also require that the functions are aestronglyMeasurable (and assign enorm = \infty otherwise)
(2) create a new definition eLpHmgNorm, which is just the same as eLpNorm, and duplicate most statements from eLpNorm to eLpHmgNorm (I know duplicating is bad, but here I don't see what else we could do)
(3) modify the definition of eLpNorm to make it non-homogeneous, by changing the behavior at p=0 and at 0<p<1. Adjust the assumptions accordingly in the statements.
Note that (3) could be split into: (3'): change at p=0; (3'') change at 0<p<1

As you can see, your PR would be perfect for (3'), but I'm not sure the library is ready for it now, because we haven't implemented (1) or (2).
In this respect, I think your proposition to implement (1) makes perfect sense. @Floris van Doorn, what do you think?

Mulling this over, I think we indeed need the duplication, and your plan to do this refactor sounds good. I also agree that Felix' PR is unfortunately not the right first step towards this new end-state.

Just checking that we agree on the following:

  • eLpNorm f μ p = eLpHmgNorm f μ p = ∞ for f non-measurable, also when p = 0, right?
  • Felix mentioned that eLpNorm will only be defined for codomains that are topological spaces in order to use AEStronglyMeasurable. This is not a problem at all.
  • How do we define MemLp? I think we should define it as eLpNorm f μ p < ∞. (This should be equivalent to eLpHmgNorm f μ p < ∞ except for p = 0.)
  • Of course, we will not duplicate the definition of MemLp or lemmas that depend on it (there are currently a bit over 200 declarations that use eLpNorm and a bit more than 400 that use MemLp).
6 messages were moved from this topic to #mathlib4 > real-valued eLpNorm by Floris van Doorn.
I agree with everything Floris writes above.
I have now opened #42406, which as originally suggested sets the eLp norm to be infinity, when the function is not almost everywhere strongly measurable
